title: Tadpole
full_review:
A precocious 15-year-old decides to divulge his secret love for his stepmother in the questionable comedy-drama "Tadpole" (Miramax).

Oscar Grubman (Aaron Stanford) speaks French fluently. He adores Voltaire and is conversant in the classics. He pays attention to what a woman's hands reveal about her. He is also 15 years old. And this weekend, home from his posh boarding school to his dad's New York City apartment for Thanksgiving, he plans to profess his love to Eve (Sigourney Weaver), his stepmother. But things become complicated when Oscar is seduced by Diane (Bebe Neuwirth), Eve's 40-something best friend.

Director Gary Winick's film is a story about teen-age angst and unrequited love with some touching as well as humorous moments. Its bubbly tone mostly masks the underlying seediness of a very early May-very late December romance. However, though the seduction of a teen-ager is criticized, it is nonetheless quite off-putting.

When the transgression is revealed, Eve's shock and disappointment are almost more than Oscar can stand. Nevertheless, he goes through with his plan to declare his love to Eve, causing her a moment of confusion and dismay. For all his sophisticated airs, Oscar is experiencing what virtually all older teens go through: first love. Eve recognizes this and does the mature thing of stopping it in its tracks yet lets Oscar down easy.

The script, written by Heather McGowan and Niels Mueller, procures some comedy from the brief love affair with catty references to "The Graduate" and 40-15 tennis scores. New York City locations are evident, but the dark, grainy digital camerawork weighs the film down.

But it is a redeeming factor in the film that Eve chastises Diane and finds the whole affair repellent -- even when Diane snaps back, "If you hadn't met someone in a very long time who was excited about life, you would consider a 15-year-old." And by the film's end, Oscar has grown up a bit and the incident has strengthened the struggling relationship between Eve and her husband (John Ritter).

However, one can't shake the feeling that the whole story is some male adolescent fantasy. The actors do a fine job with the limited roles, but the film is artificial in its construction and superficial in its philosophical and moral outlook. One can say that the so-called "chick flicks" are easily distinguishable by their sappy tone and heavy-handed focus on relationships. But films like "Tadpole" are rarely given a gender specification. A story such as this one, even when it's played for laughs, nonetheless seems to be courting a male audience, and for all the wrong reasons.

Due to an implied sexual encounter with a minor, a scene of underage drinking and fleeting rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion picture Association of America rating is PG-13- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.

This more "normal" couple acts as a foil for the first, contrasting the average fights between husband and wife to Yvan and Charlotte's problems of movie-star jealousies.

Attal finds humor in other situations as well such as dance club bouncers, nosy strangers and superficial acting classes. But the material is stretched thin and becomes a bit monotonous. And while a particular nude scene may draw guffaws from some viewers, others may be a bit startled by its brashness.
